records.value: Introduce vocabulary with a gesture: hold up a flat hand and slide it, then turn it round flat on the desk (both direct), versus flip it over so the palm faces down (opposite). Write both terms on the board with colour coding — DIRECT in blue, OPPOSITE in red. Say verbatim: 'In your table, I want a mathematical reason in column 3, not just the word yes or no. A reason like: because the order of the vertices keeps the same sense (direct), or because the order of the vertices is reversed (opposite).' Give 8 minutes for the table and worked example. Then cold-call 2 learners for part (a), 2 for part (b), and 1 for part (c) — 5 different learners. After part (c) answer, pose to the class: 'Hands down — think for 12 seconds. Some of you expected a turned shape to need flipping. Why does it not?' After 12 seconds, take 3 volunteer responses before giving the teacher explanation: rotation keeps the order of the vertices going the same way round (P→Q→R and P'→Q'→R' are both anticlockwise), so no flipping is needed — that is direct congruence. Only a reflection reverses the order (anticlockwise becomes clockwise), which is the signature of opposite congruence.

Lesson 1 — PREDICT: "What is happening to the clock hand?" | Learners observe the anchoring phenomenon (clock tower video/image sequence). In groups they predict what has changed and what has stayed the same. They sketch the hand at each position and attempt to describe the motion in their own words. The teacher records predictions on the Driving Question Board (DQB). Key vocabulary — centre, angle, direction, clockwise, anticlockwise — is introduced through discussion. Learners use an improvised clock (a card arrow pinned to a board) to demonstrate and discover that distance from centre is preserved.

Lesson 2 — OBSERVE & EXPLORE: "Discovering the Properties of Rotation" | Learners use paper cutouts of plane figures (triangles, quadrilaterals) and a pin (as the centre of rotation) to physically rotate objects through specified angles on plain paper. They record observations: object and image are congruent; every point moves through the same angle; the centre is the only invariant point; direction matters. Groups share findings and a class list of Properties of Rotation is compiled and added to the DQB. Connection to the posho mill supporting phenomenon is made.

Lesson 3 — EXPLAIN & PRACTISE: "Rotating Objects on a Plane Surface" | Learners use a geometrical set (ruler, compass, protractor) to construct the image of a given object under a specified rotation (centre and angle given) on plain paper. Step-by-step construction method is developed collaboratively: locate centre, draw rays from centre through each vertex, measure the angle, mark the image vertex at equal distance. Multiple examples with different centres (inside, outside, on the object) and angles (90°, 180°, 270°) are practised. Learners connect this to the clock-hand phenomenon — the centre of the clock is always fixed.

Lesson 4 — EXPLAIN & PRACTISE: "Rotation on the Cartesian Plane" | Learners transfer the construction skill to the Cartesian plane. Using coordinate grids, they rotate objects about the origin and about other specified centres through 90°, 180°, and 270° (clockwise and anticlockwise). They discover and record coordinate rules (e.g., 90° anticlockwise about the origin: (x, y) → (−y, x)) through guided pattern-spotting. The Kasarani football rolling phenomenon is revisited — learners calculate where a marked point would appear after a 90° and 180° rotation.

Lesson 5 — INVESTIGATE: "Finding the Centre and Angle of Rotation" | Given only an object and its image (no centre or angle provided), learners use perpendicular bisector construction to locate the centre of rotation and a protractor to measure the angle. Group investigation on plain paper and Cartesian plane. Results are verified by rotating the object using the found centre and angle and checking it maps onto the image. Learners return to the DQB and update: "We can work backwards — find the centre and angle from the evidence."

Lesson 6 — EXPLORE: "Rotational Symmetry of Plane Figures and Solids" | Learners use paper cutouts of regular polygons (equilateral triangle, square, regular hexagon — connecting to patterns on a Maasai kiondo basket) to locate points of rotational symmetry and determine the order of rotational symmetry for each figure. They then collect or examine models of 3-D solids (pyramids, triangular prisms, cones, tetrahedrons — connecting to the Rift Valley windmill phenomenon) and identify the axis and order of rotational symmetry for each solid. Findings are recorded in a class table on the DQB.

Lesson 7 — EXPLAIN: "Rotation and Congruence" | Learners use pairs of object-and-image cutouts from previous lessons to classify the type of congruence produced by rotation (direct congruence — the image fits the object by sliding and turning while it stays flat, like translation). They compare this with congruence from reflection (opposite — the image fits only after being flipped over). A sorting activity consolidates understanding. Learners connect to the clock: the hour hand at 3:00 and at 9:00 are congruent — and one is a rotation of the other, not a reflection, so they are directly congruent.

Lesson 8 — MODEL BUILDING, APPLICATION & ASSESSMENT: "Putting It All Together" | Learners revisit the anchoring phenomenon: given the clock hand position at 12:00 on a coordinate grid, they calculate its exact position at 12:15, 12:30, 12:45, and 1:00 using rotation rules. They then complete a structured class activity covering all seven SLOs: rotate an object on the Cartesian plane, find a centre and angle of rotation, determine rotational symmetry order of a given figure and solid, and identify congruence from rotation. Final DQB review: learners articulate a full answer to the driving question in writing. Real-life appreciation task: identify two examples of rotation in their school or home environment in Nairobi/their locality and describe the centre, angle, and order of symmetry.

records.value:
• The rotating blades of a maize grinding mill (posho mill) in a Kericho market: learners observe that each blade tip traces a circle around a fixed axle — prompting questions about the centre of rotation, the angle swept per second, and the symmetry of the blade arrangement.

Say: 'You are looking at the clock on the Administration Block of the University of Nairobi. It is 12:00. The minute hand is pointing straight up. In your groups, predict where the tip of the hand will be after 15, 30 and 45 minutes, and what will stay exactly the same about the hand as it moves. Sketch your prediction. You have 3 minutes.' [START TIMER — 3 minutes group work.] Circulate and listen. Do NOT confirm or correct predictions. After 3 minutes: 'One prediction from each group, please. Say: 'This is the big question that drives our entire unit. Your sticky notes are steps towards answering it.' records.value: Distribute a clean blank clock-face sheet (or direct learners to a fresh page). Say: 'This is the start of your Rotation Model Journal. Sketch the Nairobi clock hand at 12:00, 12:15, 12:30 and 12:45. Label the centre of rotation. Show the direction of rotation with an arrow. Then write your Model Statement: What kind of motion is this? What makes it different from a translation — a slide — or a reflection — a flip?' Allow 6 minutes individual work (learners finish copying the four anchor questions if they have not done so). Circulate and look at 5–6 learners' sketches. After 6 minutes, cold-call 2 learners to read their Model Statement aloud. Synthesise: 'The hand is not sliding — it is not moving in a straight line. It is not flipping — it is not producing a mirror image. It is turning about a fixed point. In mathematics, we call this a ROTATION. Write the word ROTATION at the top of your Model Journal page and underline it.' Close the lesson: 'Next lesson we ask: how much has the hand turned, and how do we measure that exactly? Look again at the clock images tonight and think how you could measure the turning.' Record this as a 'To Investigate' prompt at the bottom of the DQB.

records.why: Mark's rule (Mathematics has no 80-minute double lessons; KICD provides none): lesson shortened to 40 minutes by condensing activities, no KICD outcome dropped. Observe cut to 15 minutes: rounds shared between two pairs in each group and pooled; all four rounds and Q1 to Q4 kept.
records.value: Groups of four receive a materials pack: one A3 plain paper sheet, one triangle cutout (labelled ABC) and one quadrilateral cutout (labelled PQRS) made from card, one drawing pin, one ruler (30 cm), one protractor, and two pencils. A task card guides the investigation. The group works as two pairs and pools results in one group observation table. Set-up (both pairs): mark a centre point O on the A3 paper, put the paper on a piece of cardboard or soft board, make a small hole in the cutout, lay the hole over O and push the pin through so the cutout turns freely about O (the pin is the centre of rotation). Trace the starting position and label it 'Object'. Pair 1, Round 1: rotate triangle ABC 90° clockwise about O, trace it as 'Image 1', and measure (a) all three sides and all three angles of Object and Image 1, (b) OA and OA′, OB and OB′, OC and OC′, (c) angle AOA′, angle BOB′ and angle COC′. Pair 1, Round 3: rotate 90° anticlockwise ('Image 3') and measure OA and OA′, angle AOA′ and one side and one angle. Pair 2, Round 2: rotate triangle ABC 180° clockwise ('Image 2') and measure OA and OA′, angle AOA′, and one side and one angle. Pair 2, Round 4: use quadrilateral PQRS for one rotation of the pair's choice and measure OP and OP′, angle POP′ and one side. The two pairs copy each other's results into the group table. The group then answers four analysis questions in full sentences in their exercise books: (Q1) 'Are the object and each image congruent? How do you know?' (Q2) 'Did the pin point O move at any point? What does this tell you?' (Q3) 'Compare angle AOA′, BOB′, and COC′ in Round 1 (and AOA′ in Rounds 2 and 3). What do you notice?' (Q4) 'Compare Image 1 (90° clockwise) with Image 3 (90° anticlockwise). What is different? What does this tell you about direction?'
records.old: Groups of four or five receive a materials pack: one A3 plain paper sheet, one triangle cutout (labelled ABC) and one quadrilateral cutout (labelled PQRS) made from card, one drawing pin, one ruler (30 cm), one protractor, and two pencils. Step-by-step task card guides the investigation across four rounds. Round 1: Place triangle ABC on the A3 paper. Mark a centre point O near the centre of the paper. Put the A3 paper on a piece of cardboard or soft board. Mark a point inside the cutout and make a small hole at that point with the pin. Lay the cutout so that its hole is exactly over O, and push the pin through the hole and the paper into the cardboard, so the cutout can turn freely about O (the pin is the centre of rotation). Trace the triangle in its starting position — label it 'Object'. Rotate the cutout 90° clockwise about O. Trace the new position — label it 'Image 1'. Measure: (a) all three sides of Object and Image 1; (b) all three angles of Object and Image 1; (c) the distance OA and OA′, OB and OB′, OC and OC′; (d) angle AOA′, angle BOB′, angle COC′ using the protractor. Record all measurements in the group observation table. Round 2: Repeat for 180° clockwise rotation — label 'Image 2'. Round 3: Repeat for 90° anticlockwise rotation — label 'Image 3'. In Rounds 2 and 3 measure only OA and OA′, angle AOA′, and one side and one angle of the figure (the full set of measurements in Round 1 is enough to see the pattern; the other rounds test whether it repeats). Round 4: use quadrilateral PQRS for one rotation of the group's choice and measure OP and OP′, angle POP′, and one side. After all rounds, each group discusses and answers four analysis questions on the task card: (Q1) 'Are the object and each image congruent? How do you know?' (Q2) 'Did the pin point O move at any point? What does this tell you?' (Q3) 'Compare angle AOA′, BOB′, and COC′ in Round 1 (and AOA′ in Rounds 2 and 3). What do you notice?' (Q4) 'Compare Image 1 (90° clockwise) with Image 3 (90° anticlockwise). What is different? What does this tell you about direction?' Groups record answers in full sentences in their exercise books.

records.value: Learners work in pre-assigned groups of four, as two pairs. Each group receives: (a) Investigation Sheet 1 — plain paper with triangle PQR and image triangle P'Q'R' printed clearly (P→P', Q→Q', R→R' are labelled corresponding vertices); (b) Investigation Sheet 2 — a Cartesian plane (grid from −8 to 8 on both axes) with quadrilateral ABCD and image A'B'C'D' plotted; (c) a geometrical set (ruler, compass, protractor, set-square). Pair 1 takes Sheet 1 and Pair 2 takes Sheet 2; each pair follows the same four printed steps. STEP 1 — Draw the segment joining a vertex to its image (PP' or AA'). Construct its perpendicular bisector with compass and ruler. Label it ℓ₁. STEP 2 — Draw the segment for a second vertex (QQ' or BB') and construct its perpendicular bisector, ℓ₂. records.value: Time each report strictly: 'Group — 45 seconds starting now.' After three reports, say: 'Different groups, different shapes, but the same method worked every time. Why does that method always work?' Pause 10 seconds. Write the key statement on the board as learners dictate it: 'The perpendicular bisector of the segment joining any object point to its corresponding image point under a rotation passes through the centre of rotation.' Underline 'any' and ask: 'Why does it work for ANY pair, not just a special one?' Cold-call 1 learner. Give 1 minute of group thinking for the three deepening questions, then take one answer per question from the whole class. Q1: one bisector gives a line of possible centres; a second bisector narrows it to a unique point. Q2: Wanjiku is wrong — one bisector gives a locus, not a unique point. Q3: the perpendicular bisectors meet at the midpoint of each segment joining a point to its image, so the centre is that midpoint and the angle measures 180°. For the Consolidation Check, give 2 minutes, circulate rapidly, and note how many learners have the correct centre marked with arcs visible and how many only guessed without construction.

records.value: Introduce vocabulary with a gesture: hold up a flat hand and slide it, then turn it round flat on the desk (both direct), versus flip it over so the palm faces down (opposite). Write both terms on the board with colour coding — DIRECT in blue, OPPOSITE in red. Say verbatim: 'In your table, I want a mathematical reason in column 3, not just the word yes or no. A reason like: because the order of the vertices keeps the same sense (direct), or because the order of the vertices is reversed (opposite).' Give 6 minutes for the table and worked example. Then cold-call 1 learner for part (a), 1 for part (b) and 1 for part (c). After part (c), pose to the class: 'Hands down — think for 10 seconds. Some of you expected a turned shape to need flipping. Why does it not?' Take 2 volunteer responses before giving the teacher explanation: rotation keeps the order of the vertices going the same way round (P→Q→R and P'→Q'→R' are both anticlockwise), so no flipping is needed — that is direct congruence. Only a reflection reverses the order (anticlockwise becomes clockwise), which is the signature of opposite congruence.
